title: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
summary: Test Android and iOS apps the way MASVS and MASTG describe: packages, static and dynamic analysis, Frida, intents, providers, deep links, WebViews, biometrics, backend APIs and attestation.
outcomes: Choose MAS testing profiles from a threat model and name findings by MASVS control, MASWE weakness and MASTG test
Unpack and decompile an APK, triage its manifest and inventory the endpoints an IPA or APK references
Set up a lab device with a proxy and explain what Frida instrumentation can observe and change
Find and fix exported-component, intent redirection, file-name and deep link flaws in Android and iOS apps
Secure WebView bridges and explain the TikTok CVE-2022-28799 chain step by step
Explain why biometric unlock must be crypto-bound, and write the Keystore and Keychain fixes
Test what a backend enforces versus what the app hides, using the Grindr location cases
Explain what App Attest and Play Integrity prove, verify them server-side, and state their limits

lessons.title: The attacker holds the phone: OWASP MAS and its threat model

blocks.md:
A web application's code runs on a server you control. A mobile app's code runs on a phone you do not control: every string, every check and every hidden button ships to whoever installs it.

Tiny example. A coffee app gives 10 loyalty points per purchase. The redeem screen hides a *Redeem 500* button from users with fewer than 500 points. A tester points the phone at an intercepting proxy (a tool on their laptop that shows and can edit every request; lesson 4), sees the request `POST /redeem {"points": 500}`, and sends it from an account holding 20 points. If the server does not check the balance itself, the hidden button was never a control. The app decided what to *show*; only the server can decide what is *allowed*.

This course is about testing apps for mistakes like that one, using the standard the industry uses. The prerequisite course *Wireless and mobile security* introduced it in its storage and networking lessons: the **OWASP MAS** project (Mobile Application Security, from OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project). It has three parts:

- **MASVS**, the Mobile Application Security Verification Standard: *what must be true* of a secure app, as numbered controls.
- **MASWE**, the Mobile Application Security Weakness Enumeration: *what goes wrong*, as named weaknesses.
- **MASTG**, the Mobile Application Security Testing Guide: *how to check*, as techniques, tools and numbered tests.

The prerequisite course covered MASVS-STORAGE and MASVS-NETWORK (secrets on disk, TLS and pinning). We assume that and cover the rest.

MASVS groups its controls into eight areas:

- **STORAGE**: sensitive data at rest. **CRYPTO**: cryptography and key management.
- **AUTH**: authentication and authorization, including local authentication such as biometrics.
- **NETWORK**: data in transit.
- **PLATFORM**: interaction with the platform and other apps: IPC (inter-process communication), WebViews and the user interface.
- **CODE**: data processing, untrusted input and keeping the app and its components up to date.
- **RESILIENCE**: resistance to reverse engineering and tampering.
- **PRIVACY**: minimising, and being transparent about, personal data.

Each control is written `MASVS-AREA-n`, for example MASVS-PLATFORM-2: "The app uses WebViews securely."

blocks.title: Who attacks a mobile app, and from where

scenes.caption: The app talks to its backend. Each attacker position on this map is a different threat, and each needs different tests.
Another app on the same phone can send the app intents, links and files. The sandbox keeps it out of the app's files, not out of the app's front doors.
A network attacker sits between app and API. The prerequisite course covered this one: TLS validation and pinning.
Someone with the device itself: a thief, a forensic examiner, or malware with root. They read files and memory directly.
The user is the attacker: they own the phone, can root it, decompile the app and change it while it runs. Cheaters and fraudsters live here.
And anyone can skip the app entirely and call the API with their own client. Whatever the app hides, the backend must still enforce.

blocks.md:
Not every app needs defending against every position. MAS turns the map into **MAS Testing Profiles**, each with a stated attacker model:

- **MAS-L1** (Essential Security): "Other applications installed on the device are adversaries."
- **MAS-L2** (Advanced Security): "The operating system cannot be trusted, and attackers may have physical access to the device."
- **MAS-R** (Resilient Security): "The user of the device is an attacker, including reverse engineers and cheaters."
- **MAS-P** (Baseline Privacy): not attacker-centric; protects users' personal data.

The project's examples: a news app is L1+P; an ad-supported weather app adds R to protect ad revenue; a messenger or health app is L2+P; a banking or game app is L2+P+R. The old verification levels L1, L2 and R were reworked into profiles in the 2023 MASVS refactoring and the 2026 MASWE refactoring. Specialised profiles also exist, such as MAS-EUDIW for the EU Digital Identity Wallet.

Treat everything inside the app as readable and changeable by its user. The app's job is to protect the user's data from *other* parties (other apps, thieves, the network). Decisions about what a user is allowed to do belong on the server.

Misconception: "no root detection" is automatically a finding. MASVS states that the absence of resilience measures "does not in itself constitute a vulnerability". It matters only when the profile includes MAS-R, for example to protect against fraud or cheating.

blocks.question: A mobile game sells in-game coins. The studio worries that players will modify the app to unlock paid items for free. Which MAS testing profile is aimed at that attacker?
options: MAS-L1, because other installed apps are the adversary
MAS-L2, because the operating system cannot be trusted
MAS-R, because the user of the device is the attacker
MAS-P, because coins are personal data
blocks.explain: MAS-R's attacker model is the device's own user, including reverse engineers and cheaters. L1 and L2 protect the user from other parties; P is about personal data. Note that R only slows cheaters down: the coin balance itself must still live on the server.

blocks.question: A tester's report on a news-reading app lists 'App does not detect rooted devices' as a high-severity finding. What is the best review comment?
options: Downgrade or drop it: for an L1+P app, missing resilience controls are not in themselves a vulnerability
Keep it high: every app must block rooted devices under MASVS-STORAGE
Keep it, but rename it to M9 Insecure Data Storage
Replace it with a request to add certificate pinning
blocks.explain: MASVS-RESILIENCE says the absence of these measures does not itself constitute a vulnerability; they apply when the threat model includes the user as attacker (MAS-R). A news app is the project's own example of L1+P. Root detection is not a storage control, and pinning answers a network threat.

lessons.title: Inside an APK and an IPA: what anyone can download and read

blocks.md:
Every assessment starts with the file the store delivers. Anyone can get it, so anything inside it is public. The prerequisite course showed that an APK (the Android install file) is a ZIP archive and that secrets compiled into it can be read. Here we open one properly.

Our specimen is **UnCrackable Level 1**, a practice app that OWASP publishes for exactly this purpose (the MAS Crackmes, lesson 13). Listing the archive needs nothing but `unzip`:

blocks.code:
$ unzip -l UnCrackable-Level1.apk
  Length      Date    Time    Name
---------  ---------- -----   ----
     1648  00-00-1980 00:00   AndroidManifest.xml
     1319  00-00-1980 00:00   META-INF/CERT.RSA
     1139  00-00-1980 00:00   META-INF/CERT.SF
     1077  00-00-1980 00:00   META-INF/MANIFEST.MF
     5528  00-00-1980 00:00   classes.dex
     1260  00-00-1980 00:00   res/layout/activity_main.xml
      456  00-00-1980 00:00   res/menu/menu_main.xml
     4751  00-00-1980 00:00   res/mipmap-hdpi-v4/ic_launcher.png
   (four more launcher icons)
     2748  00-00-1980 00:00   resources.arsc
---------                     -------
    66748                     13 files
blocks.caption: Real output (four icon lines shortened). The whole app is 13 files; a production app has thousands, but the same parts.

blocks.title: The parts of an APK and what each tells a tester

scenes.caption: An APK is a ZIP file with a fixed layout. Nothing in it is hidden from the person who downloaded it.

AndroidManifest.xml (stored in a binary XML form) declares the package name, SDK levels (SDK: software development kit; here the Android API versions), permissions and every component other apps can reach. It is the attack surface map.
classes.dex holds the compiled code in DEX (Dalvik Executable) format. Unlike native machine code, it decompiles back to readable Java (lesson 3).
res/ and resources.arsc hold layouts, strings and configuration such as the network security config. Endpoints and keys often hide in strings.

Larger apps add lib/ with native code (.so files, compiled C or C++) for each processor type. These must be disassembled (for example with Ghidra, the NSA's open-source reverse engineering suite), which is slower work.
META-INF holds the signature. It proves which key signed the app, and that key's fingerprint is what verified links (lesson 8) are tied to.

blocks.md: **The signature.** Every Android app is signed by its developer. When installing an update, Android compares the new version's certificate with the installed one and allows the update if they match. (Since Android 9, APK Signature Scheme v3 also allows rotating to a new key that carries proof the old key trusts it.) `keytool`, part of the JDK (Java Development Kit), prints the signing certificate straight from the package:

blocks.code:
$ keytool -printcert -jarfile UnCrackable-Level1.apk
Signer #1:
Certificate #1:
Owner: CN=Jeroen Willemsen, OU=OMTG, O=OWASP, L=Amsterdam, C=NL
Issuer: CN=Jeroen Willemsen, OU=OMTG, O=OWASP, L=Amsterdam, C=NL
Valid from: Mon Aug 27 14:01:01 PDT 2018 until: Fri Aug 21 14:01:01 PDT 2043
Certificate fingerprints:
     SHA256: CB:E6:8A:B8:7D:64:34:1C:3F:C7:81:19:DC:12:29:E8:
             AA:86:F9:3F:DB:2C:33:AA:61:25:2F:D4:91:48:5B:1D
Signature algorithm name: SHA256withRSA
Subject Public Key Algorithm: 2048-bit RSA key
blocks.caption: Real output, trimmed (the fingerprint is wrapped onto two lines). Owner and Issuer are the same: this certificate is self-signed. Android does not ask a CA to vouch for it; what matters is that the key stays the same across updates.

blocks.md:
Two things to read from that output. First, **identity**: the app's identity on Android is the pair (package name, signing key). A repackaged copy, for example one with an instrumentation library added (lesson 5), must be re-signed with a different key, so its fingerprint changes. Second, **the SHA-256 fingerprint** is the value a website publishes to say "links to my domain may open this app" (lesson 8).

A repackaged app can still be installed by someone who sideloads it, which is why servers that care check the app's identity remotely (lesson 12) rather than trusting the app to check itself.

**The iOS package.** An iOS app ships as an `.ipa` file, also a ZIP. Unzipped, it holds a `Payload` folder with the **application bundle** (`Name.app`), which contains, per the MASTG:

- `Info.plist`: configuration as key-value pairs: bundle ID, version, custom URL schemes (`CFBundleURLTypes`), App Transport Security settings (`NSAppTransportSecurity`) and permission purpose strings (keys ending in `UsageDescription`).
- `_CodeSignature/`: a signature over every file in the bundle; the app's entitlements are embedded in the main binary's code signature.
- `Frameworks/`: the app's own dynamic libraries; `PlugIns/`: app extensions.
- The app binary itself, in Mach-O (the executable format of Apple's operating systems).

Two differences from Android matter for testers. iOS binaries are compiled to machine code, so they "can only be disassembled", not decompiled to source. And App Store binaries are **encrypted** with Apple's DRM (digital rights management): copying the binary off a device is not enough; testers obtain a decrypted copy by dumping it from memory on a jailbroken test device, or test a build the developer provides.

Legal note from the MASTG: in the US the DMCA (Digital Millennium Copyright Act, 17 U.S.C. 1201) makes circumventing some DRM illegal, with exemptions for certain security research. On a client engagement, ask the developer for unencrypted builds; it is faster and removes the question.
Compiled is not secret. DEX decompiles to near-source, native code disassembles, and resource files are plain. Design as if the package were published on the app's website, because in effect it is.

blocks.question: A client ships an update and its users report that it will not install over the old version: 'App not installed'. The release engineer used a new signing key. Why does Android refuse?
options: The new key's certificate has expired
Android compares the update's certificate with the installed app's and allows the update only if they match (or the new key was rotated in with proof from the old one)
The new APK is missing classes.dex
Google Play must countersign every certificate
blocks.explain: The package name plus the signing key are the app's identity, so an unrelated new key looks like a different author. Android's docs say a new certificate means a new package name and a separate app. The certificate in our output is self-signed and valid until 2043, so expiry and CA countersigning are not the issue.

blocks.question: You copy an App Store app's main binary from a jailbroken iPhone and open it in a disassembler, but the code section looks like random bytes. What is the most likely reason?
options: iOS binaries are compressed with ZIP
Swift code cannot be disassembled
The app is obfuscated by default by Xcode
App Store binaries are encrypted with Apple's DRM, so a decrypted copy must be dumped from memory while the app runs, or obtained from the developer
blocks.explain: The MASTG notes that because of DRM the binary is encrypted when stored on the device; pulling it from the bundle is not enough. The IPA is a ZIP, but the binary inside it is the encrypted part. Xcode does not obfuscate by default, and Swift binaries disassemble like any other.

lessons.title: Static analysis: decompile, read the manifest, search the code

blocks.md:
**Static analysis** means examining the app without running it: its manifest, code, resources and libraries. **Dynamic analysis** (lessons 4 and 5) means watching it run. Static work is fast, repeatable and finds where to look; dynamic work confirms what actually happens.

Tiny example. Searching the decompiled UnCrackable app for a few patterns takes one command, and each hit is a question for later:

blocks.code:
$ jadx -d out UnCrackable-Level1.apk
INFO  - loading ...
INFO  - processing ...
INFO  - done
$ cd out/sources
$ grep -rnoE 'https?://[^"]*|Cipher\.getInstance\("[^"]*"\)|System\.getenv\("[A-Z]+"\)|Build\.TAGS' . | sort -u
sg/vantagepoint/a/a.java:13:Cipher.getInstance("AES")
sg/vantagepoint/a/c.java:18:Build.TAGS
sg/vantagepoint/a/c.java:9:System.getenv("PATH")
blocks.caption: Real output (jadx 1.5.6). No URLs: this app has no backend. An AES cipher (where does its key come from?) and an environment lookup and a build-tag check that turn out to be root detection (lesson 12).

blocks.md:
The tools, as the MASTG describes them:

- **jadx** decompiles DEX bytecode back to Java source and decodes the binary manifest and resources. Our run produced 6 Java files and a readable `AndroidManifest.xml`. Class names like `sg.vantagepoint.a.c` are already shortened: the build renamed them (obfuscation, lesson 12), but the logic is still readable.
- **apktool** decodes resources to near-original form and can rebuild a modified APK.
- **MobSF** (Mobile Security Framework) is an automated platform that runs static and dynamic checks on Android and iOS apps and produces a report; treat its output as leads to verify.
- **semgrep** is a pattern-based code scanner for Java, Kotlin (Android's main app language today) and Swift (Apple's main iOS language). Many MASTG tests ship semgrep rules, for example MASTG-DEMO-0090 for event-bound biometrics.

For iOS, the equivalent first steps are reading `Info.plist` and the entitlements, listing linked frameworks, and disassembling the binary.

blocks.code:
<manifest package="owasp.mstg.uncrackable1" ...>
    <uses-sdk android:minSdkVersion="19" android:targetSdkVersion="28"/>
    <application ... android:allowBackup="true">
        <activity android:name="sg.vantagepoint.uncrackable1.MainActivity">
            <intent-filter>
                <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN"/>
                <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER"/>
            </intent-filter>
        </activity>
    </application>
</manifest>
blocks.caption: The manifest as jadx decoded it (labels and icon attributes trimmed). One component, the launcher screen. minSdkVersion 19 means the app installs on Android 4.4, far below current platform versions (MASVS-CODE-1).

blocks.md:
The manifest is where an Android review starts, because it lists every door. A reviewer asks:

- Is `android:debuggable="true"` set in a release build? (MASWE-0063, debug mechanisms not disabled.)
- What is the **minSdkVersion**, the oldest Android the app accepts? Old platforms lack fixes and protections.
- Which components are **exported**, meaning other apps can start them, and is each one protected by a permission? (Lesson 6.)
- Which **deep links** (intent filters with a `scheme`) does it accept, and are web links verified? (Lesson 8.)
- Does `allowBackup` let its data into backups, and is a network security config referenced?

Checks like these are easy to automate. The script below reads a decoded manifest and prints leads. We ran it on UnCrackable and on a deliberately bad example manifest written for this lesson (`shop.xml`, a fictional shopping app).

blocks.caption: manifest_triage.py, Python 3, standard library only.

blocks.code:
$ python3 manifest_triage.py uncrackable1.xml shop.xml
== owasp.mstg.uncrackable1 (minSdk 19, targetSdk 28)
  [info] allowBackup=true: check what lands in backups
  [check] activity sg.vantagepoint.uncrackable1.MainActivity: has intent filter, exported not set
== com.example.shop (minSdk 23, targetSdk 34)
  [high] android:debuggable=true in a release build
  [info] allowBackup=true: check what lands in backups
  [review] activity .PromoWebActivity: exported, no permission
  [review] deep link shopapp://promo (custom scheme, unverifiable)
  [review] receiver .SyncReceiver: exported, no permission
  [review] provider .OrdersProvider: exported, no permission
blocks.caption: Real output. Every line is a lead, not a verdict: the UnCrackable [check] is its launcher, which must be reachable anyway; an app targeting Android 12 or later must set android:exported on every component that has an intent filter, or it will not install.

blocks.title: A static review: from package to a list of leads

scenes.caption: Start from the exact file users receive, not the source tree: build steps and SDKs change what ships.
Decompile and decode. The merged manifest in the final APK includes components that libraries added, which never appear in the developer's own manifest file.
Search code and resources for endpoints, keys and risky APIs: WebView bridges, intent forwarding, crypto calls, logging.
Every lead goes on a list with the MASTG test that would confirm it. Static analysis says 'this could happen'; dynamic analysis shows whether it does.

blocks.md:
**Case: the Tea app, July 2025.** Tea Dating Advice, a US women-only dating safety app with 1.6 million users, required new members to submit a selfie and, for a time, a photo of an ID to prove they were women. In late July 2025, posts on 4chan (an anonymous message board) claimed its verification images sat in a public **Firebase** storage bucket (Firebase is Google's mobile and web app development platform) that needed no authentication. The news site Engadget reported that 404 Media, a tech news outlet, "verified that the exposed storage bucket URL matches one found in Tea's Android app".

Tea confirmed unauthorised access to "a legacy data storage system" with about 72,000 images: about 13,000 selfies and photo IDs from account verification, and 59,000 images from posts, comments and direct messages. Only users who signed up before February 2024 were affected. Its privacy policy had said verification images were "deleted immediately" ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c7vl57n74pqo)). Images then circulated on forums, and some were used to map users' locations.

What the case teaches a mobile tester:

- **The bug was not in the app's code.** It was a backend storage configuration. But the package is a map of the backend: every bucket, API host and third-party service the app talks to is written in it.
- **Static analysis therefore includes the backend inventory.** List every host and storage URL in the release build, and (within the agreed scope) check each one for anonymous access.
- **Legacy matters.** The data came from a system the company had migrated away from but not deleted.

**Defender view.** Prevent: require authentication and per-user access rules on every storage bucket; delete data you promised to delete; keep an inventory of the endpoints your shipped apps reference. Detect: storage access logs showing anonymous listing or bulk reads; an external scan of your own app's referenced endpoints in CI (continuous integration, the automated build and test pipeline). Respond: close access, determine what was read, notify affected users.

Misconception: "the URL is in the app, so it's fine to leave the bucket open: only our app knows it." Anything in the package is public (lesson 2). A storage URL, an API key or a hidden endpoint in an app is a published address.

blocks.question: The triage script flags `[review] provider .OrdersProvider: exported, no permission` in shop.xml. What is the right next step?
options: Confirm on a test device whether another app can query it and what data comes back, then map it to the MASTG content provider tests
Report it immediately as a critical data leak
Ignore it: content providers are protected by the app sandbox
Delete the provider from the manifest yourself and rebuild the app
blocks.explain: Static analysis produces leads. An exported provider without a permission may be fine (it might serve public data) or a serious leak; only querying it from another app (dynamic analysis) tells you. The sandbox protects files, not components the app chose to export. Testers report, they do not patch the client's app.

blocks.question: Which part of the Tea incident could a static review of the Android app have surfaced before attackers did?
options: The 4chan posts
The number of affected users
The legacy storage bucket's address, which was written in the app, giving a reviewer an endpoint to test for anonymous access
That the app blocks screenshots
blocks.explain: 404 Media matched the exposed bucket's URL to one found in Tea's Android app. Listing every endpoint a release build references, and testing each for unauthenticated access, is exactly the static-plus-backend step that finds this class of exposure.

lessons.title: Dynamic analysis: a test device, a proxy and the app's own files

blocks.md:
Static analysis said what *could* happen. Dynamic analysis runs the app and watches what *does*: the requests it sends, the files it writes, the messages it logs.

Tiny example. You log in to an app on a test phone, then list its private data directory. Before login there were 3 files; after login there are 5, and one of them is a crash-reporting log containing the password you just typed. No amount of reading code would have told you that a third-party logging library was recording form fields.

**The lab.** You need a device where you can see inside an app's sandbox:

- An **emulator** (for Android, an Android Virtual Device from Android Studio) or a physical **test device you own**, rooted (Android) or jailbroken (iOS). Root lets you read any app's private directory, which a normal phone forbids.
- **adb** (Android Debug Bridge), Android's command-line tool for talking to a device: open a shell, install apps, copy files, read the system log (`adb logcat`).
- An **intercepting proxy** such as Burp Suite (PortSwigger's testing proxy) or ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy). The MASTG calls this set-up Machine-in-the-Middle (MITM): the tester's machine sits between app and server and can review and modify every request and response.

Never use a phone with your real accounts on it: rooting removes protections (the prerequisite course's Android lesson), and test tools see everything.

**Getting HTTPS into the proxy.** The prerequisite course explained that apps targeting Android 7.0 (API level 24) or later trust only the *system* CA store by default, so installing the proxy's CA certificate in the *user* store does nothing for them. Testers use one of three routes, all on their own lab device:

1. Test a **debug build** whose network security config trusts user CAs only under `debug-overrides` (the developer can provide one).
2. On a rooted test device, add the proxy CA to the **system** store, as the MASTG describes.
3. If the app pins its server key, a pinned connection to the proxy fails by design; testers then use a build without pinning, or instrumentation (lesson 5) on their own build.

What defenders see: traffic from a test device looks like normal traffic from an unusual client. Server-side, nothing distinguishes a proxy user from an app user, which is the point of lesson 11.

blocks.title: An HTTPS request through an intercepting proxy on a lab device

scenes.caption: The lab phone's Wi-Fi proxy points at the tester's laptop. The app opens TLS to api.example.com, but the connection lands at the proxy.
The proxy answers with a certificate it generated for api.example.com, signed by its own CA, and opens a separate TLS connection to the real server.
Release build, proxy CA only in the user store: the app does not trust it. Handshake fails, nothing is sent. This is the protection working.
Debug build that trusts user CAs (or a system-store CA on a rooted lab phone): the handshake succeeds and the proxy can read the request.
The proxy forwards (or edits) it, the server answers, and the tester sees both sides: every endpoint, header, token and field the app uses.

blocks.md:
**Watching files and logs.** The MASTG tests for local data leaks are mostly dynamic: use every feature, then look at what the app left behind. On Android, an app's private directory is under `/data/data/<package>/` (shared_prefs, databases, files, cache). On iOS, the app's container has `Documents`, `Library/Preferences` and `Library/Caches`. Read the system log during the session too: MASTG-TEST-0203 (Android) and MASTG-TEST-0296 (iOS) check logs for sensitive data, which MASWE names *Insertion of Sensitive Data into Logs* (MASWE-0005).

A short script makes the search repeatable. Below we built a small fake app container on a laptop and scanned it.

blocks.caption: scan_container.py with its real output on a three-file test container we made (a preferences plist, a notes file, and a crash log holding a failed login). Patterns find only what you think to look for: also read new files by eye.

blocks.md:
**Case: Starbucks for iOS, 2014 (CVE-2014-0647).** Daniel Wood, a security researcher, published an advisory on 13 January 2014 for version 2.6.1 of the Starbucks iOS app, after reporting it in December 2013 with "no direct response". The app's username, email address and password were "stored in clear-text in the session.clslog crashlytics log file", at `/Library/Caches/com.crashlytics.data/com.starbucks.mystarbucks/session.clslog`. Crashlytics is a crash-reporting framework embedded in many apps; the same log also held the account's OAuth token and signature.

[iMore](https://www.imore.com/starbucks-mobile-app-has-sensitive-user-information-exposed), an Apple news site, tested it and narrowed the claim: the app's token itself was stored in the Keychain as recommended, a successful login did not appear to log the password, but failed login attempts and new sign-ups did. Its conclusion: "a single bug or oversight can undermine an otherwise sound implementation." Starbucks said it had added safeguards.

The lessons:

- **Logging is storage.** Data written to a log or crash report is data at rest, and it may also be uploaded to a third party. Wood's fix was to sanitise output so credentials never reach the log.
- **SDKs act with your app's permissions.** The developer did not write the log file; the crash reporter did, from what the app gave it.
- **Only dynamic testing shows it.** The leak depended on which screen and which outcome (failed login) occurred.

**Defender view.** Prevent: never pass credentials, tokens or form contents to logging or crash APIs; strip debug logging from release builds; review what each SDK collects. Detect: run the scan above (or MASTG tests 0203 and 0296) in CI against a test build after an automated login. Respond: ship a build that deletes the old log files, and treat any credential that reached a third party's servers as exposed.

Snapshot the app's directory before and after each feature (login, payment, logout) and diff the two. New files and changed files are where to look first. Logout is a good test: MASWE-0024 is *Sensitive Data Accessible After Session Termination*.

blocks.question: You install Burp's CA certificate in the user store of a lab phone and set the Wi-Fi proxy. A browser's traffic appears in Burp, but the shopping app (release build, targets API 34, no network security config) shows only failed handshakes. What does this tell you?
options: The app is pinning certificates, which is a vulnerability
Burp is misconfigured, because the browser would fail too
The app is using the platform default for apps targeting Android 7.0 and later: it trusts only system CAs, which is correct behaviour
The app does not use HTTPS
blocks.explain: Since API level 24, apps trust only the system store unless their network security config says otherwise; with no config they use that safe default. The browser trusts user CAs, so it works. Failed handshakes show TLS is in use and validated. Use a debug build or a system-store CA on a rooted lab device.

blocks.question: In the Starbucks case, the app kept its OAuth token in the Keychain, yet the password still leaked. Which MASVS control did the app fail?
options: MASVS-STORAGE-2: the app prevents leakage of sensitive data, here through a log file
MASVS-NETWORK-1, because the password was sent in cleartext
MASVS-RESILIENCE-1, because the phone could be jailbroken
MASVS-CRYPTO-1, because the Keychain is weak
blocks.explain: Storing the token securely satisfies part of STORAGE-1, but the password reached a log through the crash reporter: a leak, which is STORAGE-2. There was no network flaw in the advisory, and resilience controls would not stop an app from writing its own log.

lessons.title: Dynamic instrumentation with Frida: watch and change a running app

blocks.md:
A proxy shows what leaves the phone. Some questions need a view *inside* the process: which URL did the app just build, what key went into that cipher, what did the biometric callback return? **Dynamic instrumentation** answers them by inserting your own code into the running app.

Tiny example. An app sends an encrypted blob to its server, so the proxy shows only ciphertext. Instrumenting the app's call to its encryption function prints the plaintext *before* encryption: the tester now sees the real request, on their own lab device and their own build.

**Frida** is "a free and open source dynamic code instrumentation toolkit written by Ole André Vadla Ravnås" (MASTG-TOOL-0031). It injects a JavaScript engine (QuickJS in current versions) into the target process, and you write small JavaScript snippets that run inside it. It works on Android, iOS and desktop platforms.

When it attaches to a running app on a rooted device, per the MASTG:

1. Frida uses `ptrace` (the operating system's debugging interface) to take over a thread of the process and write a small bootstrapper into its memory.
2. The bootstrapper starts a new thread, connects to the Frida server running on the device, and loads the Frida agent library.
3. The agent opens a two-way channel back to the tool on the tester's computer.
4. The hijacked thread is restored and the app carries on, now with the agent inside.

blocks.title: How Frida attaches to an app on a rooted lab device (injected mode)

scenes.caption: frida-server runs as root on the lab device and listens on localhost port 27042 by default. The tester's CLI connects to it over USB.
The server uses ptrace to borrow one thread of the app and writes a bootstrapper into its memory.
The bootstrapper loads the Frida agent library, with its JavaScript engine, inside the app's own process.
The agent connects back; the borrowed thread is restored and the app keeps running. The tester's script now runs with the app's privileges and sees its memory.
Each time the app calls the hooked function, the script's code runs first and can log, or change, arguments and return values.

blocks.md:
**Three ways in.** The MASTG lists three modes:

- **Injected**: the common case above, with `frida-server` running as a daemon. It needs a rooted or jailbroken device.
- **Embedded**: on a device that is not rooted, you cannot `ptrace` another app, so the **Frida Gadget** library is packaged into the app itself, manually or with tools such as objection (a Frida-based testing toolkit, described below). The app must then be re-signed, which changes its signing fingerprint (lesson 2).
- **Preloaded**: the gadget loads automatically and runs a script from the file system, similar to `LD_PRELOAD` on Linux (an environment variable that makes the loader load a given library first).

**The main APIs.** `Interceptor` hooks a function by overwriting its first instructions with a jump to your code (a *trampoline*); the MASTG notes this "cannot be considered transparent" and can be detected, for example by apps that checksum their own code. `Stalker` traces execution by recompiling code on the fly, leaving the original untouched. The `Java` and `ObjC` bridges let scripts find and call Android Java classes and iOS Objective-C classes. Since Frida 17 those bridges are no longer bundled into the core runtime, but the command-line tools (`frida`, `frida-trace`) still ship with them.

blocks.caption: An observation-only hook: it records arguments and changes nothing. Not run here (it needs an Android device with frida-server). Use it only on apps you own or are authorised to test.

blocks.md: **What testers use it for.** Frida underlies many MASTG techniques: monitoring deep link handlers at runtime (MASTG-TECH-0173), confirming at runtime that a biometric prompt is only a boolean gate (the weakness MASWE-0020, Local Authentication Can Be Bypassed; lesson 10), inspecting what goes into crypto calls, and confirming that client-side checks can be switched off (lesson 12). Tools built on it include **frida-trace** (trace calls without writing a script) and **objection**, which its GitHub page calls "a runtime mobile exploration toolkit, powered by Frida", for exploring an app's files, memory and classes.

**Defender view.** What instrumentation looks like from the app's side: a `frida-server` process and a listener on port 27042 on a rooted device; an extra native library and a changed signing certificate in a repackaged app; modified function prologues that integrity checks can spot. Apps can look for these (MASVS-RESILIENCE-4, anti-dynamic analysis), but on a device the attacker controls every check can itself be hooked. The durable response is to stop trusting the client's answers at all: lessons 10 to 12.

On a device its user controls, any value in the app's memory and any boolean the app computes can be read and changed. Design so that changing them gains nothing: keys in secure hardware, decisions on the server.

blocks.question: A tester has a stock, non-rooted Android phone and wants to use Frida on a client's app. Which statement is right?
options: Injected mode works the same; frida-server needs no special rights
It is impossible; Frida needs root in every mode
Frida can only instrument iOS apps without root
They can use embedded mode: package Frida Gadget into the app and re-sign it, which changes the app's signing identity
blocks.explain: Without root, ptrace into another app's process is not allowed, so injected mode fails. Embedded mode puts the gadget inside the app; the repackaged app must be re-signed with a different key, which is also something servers and integrity checks can notice (lessons 2 and 12).

blocks.question: Why does the MASTG say Interceptor hooks are not transparent?
options: Interceptor overwrites the start of the hooked function with a trampoline, so the app's code in memory changes and can be detected, for example by checksumming it
Interceptor sends every hooked call over the network
Interceptor only works on Java code
Interceptor requires restarting the app for each hook
blocks.explain: Inline hooking modifies the function's first instructions to jump to the agent's code. That modification is visible to code-integrity checks. Stalker avoids it by executing recompiled copies and leaving the original code untouched.

lessons.title: Android IPC: exported components, intent redirection, PendingIntents

blocks.md:
The sandbox keeps other apps out of an app's *files*. It does not keep them away from the app's *front doors*: the components it lets other apps start. Those doors are where MASVS-PLATFORM-1, "The app uses IPC mechanisms securely", lives (IPC: inter-process communication).

Tiny example. A shopping app has a screen, `OrderDetailsActivity`, that shows the order whose id it receives. If the screen is reachable from other apps and trusts whatever id arrives, any app on the phone can open your orders, or someone else's if the server does not check (lesson 11).

**The pieces.** An Android app is built from four kinds of **components**: *activities* (screens), *services* (background work), *broadcast receivers* (listeners for system or app events) and *content providers* (data served to others, lesson 7). Components are started with an **intent**, a message object naming an action and carrying data and *extras* (key-value pairs).

- An **explicit intent** names the exact target component.
- An **implicit intent** names only an action (such as "view this link"), and the system picks a component that declared a matching **intent filter**.

The attribute `android:exported` decides whether other apps can start a component. Android's guidance: if `true`, "any app can access the activity and launch it by its exact class name"; if `false`, only the same app, apps with the same user ID, or privileged system components can. The default has changed across versions and component types, so the advice is: **always set it explicitly**. Since Android 12, an app that targets Android 12 and has a component with an intent filter but no explicit `android:exported` cannot even be installed.

**Intent redirection.** Android's own definition: it "occurs when an attacker can partly or fully control the contents of an intent used to launch a new component in the context of a vulnerable app". The pattern is an exported component that receives an intent inside an intent (often as an extra) and starts it. The inner intent then runs with the *vulnerable* app's identity, so it can reach that app's non-exported components and, with URI permission flags, its private content providers.

Android's mitigations: avoid forwarding nested intents; if unavoidable, check where the intent is going and strip the permission-granting flags (`FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION` and its siblings), for example with `IntentSanitizer`; prefer `PendingIntent` (below). Android 16 adds a default hardening against intent redirection, with an opt-out API, and apps targeting Android 12 or later can enable a StrictMode check that flags "unsafe intent launch".

blocks.caption: Kotlin. Any app can supply 'next', including an intent aimed at this app's non-exported screens or one carrying URI-grant flags for its private providers. getParcelableExtra with a class argument needs API 33; IntentCompat.getParcelableExtra covers older versions.

IntentSanitizer (AndroidX core) copies only what the allowlist names: one target component, one string extra. Grant flags and other targets are refused, so the forwarded intent can no longer reach anything else. Not compiled here.

blocks.title: Intent redirection: borrowing another app's identity

scenes.caption: A malicious app cannot open the victim app's private provider directly: it is not exported. Android refuses.
But the victim app has an exported activity that forwards an intent found in its extras. The malicious app wraps its request inside.
The forwarding activity starts 'inner' as itself. To Android, the request now comes from the victim app, which may reach its own private components and grant URI permissions.
With read or write grant flags plus the persistable flag (as in the EngageSDK case below), the malicious app gains access to the private provider and keeps it until the victim app revokes it.
Fixed: the activity is not exported, or it sanitises the inner intent against an allowlist. The inner request is rejected and nothing is granted.

blocks.md: **Case: EngageSDK, 2025 to 2026.** Microsoft researchers found an intent redirection flaw in **EngageSDK**, a third-party Android SDK from EngageLab for push notifications and messaging. Adding the library put an exported activity, `MTCommonActivity`, into apps' **merged manifest**, the final manifest the build produces after combining the app's own with every library's, so developers "sometimes missed" it. The activity read a URI from the incoming intent, parsed a JSON field from it, and built an intent from a nested string using a parsing flag (`URI_ALLOW_UNSAFE`) that permits URI-permission grants; it then started that intent with the app's identity. Another app on the device could thereby gain persistent read and write access to the vulnerable app's content providers, including non-exported ones, and so to its private data.

Many affected apps were crypto wallets: over 30 million installations for wallets alone and over 50 million in total. Microsoft reported it to EngageLab in April 2025 and to the Android Security Team in May 2025. Version 5.2.1, released 3 November 2025, made the activity non-exported. Detected vulnerable apps were removed from Google Play, Android added protections for already-installed apps, and Microsoft said it had seen no exploitation in the wild.

**PendingIntent.** A `PendingIntent` is a token that lets app A give app B the right to perform a predefined action *as app A*, for example when a notification is tapped. If it is **mutable**, B can fill in fields A left empty, including the target, and reach A's non-exported components. Android's guidance: set the action, component and package explicitly and use `FLAG_IMMUTABLE`. Adding `FLAG_ONE_SHOT` also makes the token usable only once, for actions that must not be replayed.

```
PendingIntent.getActivity(context, 0,
    Intent(context, OrderDetailsActivity::class.java),
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_ONE_SHOT)
```

**Defender view.** Prevent: explicit `android:exported` on every component, permissions (signature level for partner apps) on those that must be public, no nested-intent forwarding, immutable PendingIntents. Detect: review the *merged* manifest of every release in CI (Android Lint, the static checker in Android's build tools, can flag several of these), and run MASTG-TEST-0364 to 0366 for exported activities, services and receivers. **drozer**, an Android testing framework, plays the role of another app interacting with "other apps' IPC endpoints", which is exactly this test. Respond: ship an update that unexports the component; for SDK bugs, upgrade the SDK and check every app that embeds it.

Misconception: "we never exported that activity, so it is not exported." Libraries add components to the merged manifest at build time. Review the manifest of the APK you ship (lesson 3), not the one in your repository.

blocks.question: Your app forwards an intent from an extra, but only after checking `next.component?.packageName == packageName`. Is that enough?
options: Yes: if the target is inside our own app, nothing can go wrong

No: forwarding to the app's own non-exported components is exactly the danger, and grant flags or extras can still be attacker-chosen; allowlist the specific component and extras and strip grant flags
Yes, as long as the activity is exported
No, because package names can be spoofed by the sender
blocks.explain: Intent redirection is dangerous precisely because the target is inside your app: the attacker borrows your identity to reach your private components and providers. Checking 'it is our package' lets all of that through. Android's guidance is to check the exact destination and clear the URI-grant flags, as IntentSanitizer does.

blocks.question: Why did the EngageSDK flaw affect apps whose developers never wrote an exported activity?
options: Because Android exports every activity by default since Android 12
Because the SDK modified the app's code at runtime
Because the library's own manifest added an exported activity to each app's merged manifest during the build
Because Google Play exports components after upload
blocks.explain: Microsoft explains that MTCommonActivity was added to the merged manifest when the library was imported, appearing only after the build, which is why developers missed it. Android 12 made the exported attribute mandatory for components with intent filters; it did not export everything.

lessons.title: Content providers and shared files: from URI grants to Dirty Stream

blocks.md:
Apps share data through **content providers**, the fourth component type. A provider answers requests for `content://` URIs, much as a web server answers `https://` URLs. Microsoft's example: an app `com.example.server` that shares files from its `files/images` directory under the name `shared_images` serves them at

`content://[authority]/shared_images/[sub-path]/[filename]`

where the **authority** is the provider's system-wide name. Android ships a ready-made one for files, **FileProvider**. The usual way to share is a **URI grant**: the sharing app sends an intent carrying a content URI plus `FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION` (or write), giving the receiver temporary access to that one item without exporting the provider.

Providers fail in three common ways, each with MASTG tests:

- **Exported with no permission**, so any app can query everything (MASTG-TEST-0355 and 0356, unauthorised database access through providers).
- **SQL injection**: providers backed by SQLite (a small database library that keeps its tables in a file inside the app) that build queries from the caller's selection or path (MASTG-TEST-0339). SQL injection means the caller's text is pasted into a database query and changes what the query does. The fix is to pass the caller's values as parameters (selection arguments with `?` placeholders), never by string concatenation.
- **Oversharing**: a FileProvider whose path configuration exposes the whole data directory instead of one folder (MASTG-TEST-0357).

The fourth failure is on the *receiving* side, and it is the one that hit apps with billions of installs.

**Trusting the sender's file name.** When an app receives a shared file, it usually asks the sending provider for the file's metadata, including `_display_name`, then copies the stream into its own storage. If it uses that name as the destination path, the *sender* chooses where the file lands. A name such as `../../shared_prefs/settings.xml` walks out of the inbox folder (`..` means "parent directory") into the receiving app's settings. Microsoft named this pattern **Dirty Stream**. A malicious app does not need the user's help: it can send an explicit intent with its own provider's URI straight to a share target.

blocks.title: Dirty Stream: a share target writes where the sender says

scenes.caption: A malicious app sends an explicit SEND intent straight to a share target's exported activity, attaching a content URI that points at its own provider.
The share target asks the sender's provider for the file's name and size, as most share targets do.
The malicious provider answers with a relative path instead of a plain name. The share target does not check it.
The share target opens its inbox plus that name and copies the stream: the file lands in its own private settings, which it trusts.
Fixed: the share target ignores the name and writes to a random file in its inbox, or canonicalises the path and rejects anything outside the inbox.

blocks.caption: Java (what Android apps compile from, alongside Kotlin). The main method that prints the output below is left out to fit. It only computes paths; nothing is written.

blocks.code:
$ javac SafeCache.java && java SafeCache
name:     photo.jpg
  weak:   /data/data/com.example.share/files/inbox/photo.jpg
  checked:/data/data/com.example.share/files/inbox/photo.jpg
name:     ../../shared_prefs/settings.xml
  weak:   /data/data/com.example.share/shared_prefs/settings.xml
  checked:rejected: ../../shared_prefs/settings.xml
random:   36-char random name
blocks.caption: Real output (JDK 25 on a laptop; the paths follow Android's layout but are only computed). The weak version resolves to the app's own shared_prefs; the checked version refuses. Appending the separator to the prefix stops 'inbox-evil/' from passing as 'inbox'.

blocks.md: **Case: Dirty Stream, 2024.** Microsoft published the pattern in a blog post on 1 May 2024 (its references cite an earlier Black Hat Asia 2023 talk on it) after finding it in several Google Play apps "that represented over four billion installations", including Xiaomi's File Manager (over 1 billion installs) and WPS Office (over 500 million).

In Xiaomi File Manager, an exported copy activity accepted a content URI, and its validity check (written for file paths) always passed for content URIs. Names from the sender's provider then placed files inside the app's private directory. Microsoft chained that with how the app loaded a native library (it would load a copy from its writable data directory if a hash stored in its preferences matched) and how Android's `SharedPreferences` restores a `.bak` file, and obtained **code execution as the file manager**. The app also stored its users' SMB and FTP file-share credentials (Server Message Block and File Transfer Protocol, protocols for network file shares) in cleartext, so the impact reached the user's local network. Xiaomi fixed it in version V1-210593 and WPS in 17.0.0; Microsoft says fixes were deployed as of February 2024, and Google published developer guidance on untrustworthy provider file names.

Microsoft's fixes for share targets:

- "Completely ignore the name returned by the remote file provider when caching the received content"; random names are the most robust approach.
- If a name is needed, sanitise it and check with `File.getCanonicalPath` that the result is inside the dedicated directory.
- Do not extract names with `Uri.getLastPathSegment()`, which URL-decodes, so `%2F` becomes `/`.
- The case also shows why native libraries belong only in the app's protected library directory, never in writable storage; Microsoft points to Android Lint's check for unsafe dynamically loaded code.

**Defender view.** Detect: Android Lint and CodeQL (GitHub's code query engine) checks in CI; a test that shares a file with a `../` display name to your app and checks where it lands. Respond: users of an app with this flaw should update; Microsoft also advised resetting credentials stored by the vulnerable file manager.
A shared file arrives with two attacker-controlled things: its content and its name. Treat both as untrusted input. Choose your own name, and parse the content as hostile.

blocks.question: A share target checks the raw URI string for `../` and, finding none, saves the file under `uri.lastPathSegment`. A tester sends `content://evil/..%2F..%2Fshared_prefs%2Fx.xml`. What happens?
options: The check blocks it, because the URI contains '..'
The file is saved under the literal encoded name '..%2F..%2Fshared_prefs%2Fx.xml' inside the inbox
Android rejects content URIs that contain percent signs
The raw string has no '../', so the check passes; getLastPathSegment then decodes %2F to '/', and the name walks out of the inbox
blocks.explain: Microsoft warns that getLastPathSegment returns the URL-decoded last segment. Checking the encoded form and using the decoded form is a classic mismatch. The robust fixes do not depend on spotting bad characters: a random name, or a canonical-path check that the result lies inside the inbox.

blocks.question: Why is the canonical-path check in SafeCache written against `INBOX.getCanonicalPath() + File.separator` rather than just the inbox path?
options: Without the trailing separator, a sibling directory such as 'inbox-evil' would also start with the inbox path and pass the check
Because getCanonicalPath removes the last character
Because Android paths use backslashes
It makes no difference; it is style
blocks.explain: String prefix checks on paths must end at a directory boundary. '/files/inbox-evil/x' starts with '/files/inbox' but not with '/files/inbox/'. Android uses forward slashes; File.separator is '/' there.

lessons.title: Deep links: custom schemes, App Links and Universal Links

blocks.md:
A **deep link** is a URI that opens a specific place inside an app instead of its home screen. Tapping `shopapp://promo?code=SPRING` in a message could open the shop's promotion screen with the code filled in; tapping `https://shop.example.com/orders/1142` could open order 1142 in the app rather than the website.

Deep links are input from outside. Anyone can write a link, put it in a web page, an email or a QR code, and have another person's phone deliver it to your app. Two questions follow: *which app receives the link?* and *what does the app do with what's inside it?* MASWE calls failures here *Insecure Deep Links* (MASWE-0029).

**Custom URL schemes** (`shopapp://`) are the oldest kind. An app declares the scheme (on Android in an intent filter, on iOS under `CFBundleURLTypes` in Info.plist) and the system routes matching links to it. Nothing checks who owns a scheme:

- On Android, if two apps claim the same link, the system shows a **disambiguation dialog** and the user may pick the wrong app; the MASTG calls this *deep link collision*.
- On iOS, the MASTG notes that "an app installed after the original app may declare the same scheme and the system might target all new requests to the last installed app".

So a custom scheme is fine for opening a screen, but never for delivering something secret, such as an OAuth authorization code (the prerequisite API course showed that interception attack and PKCE, its fix).

**Verified links** fix the *which app* question by tying an `https` link to a domain the developer controls.

- **Android App Links** (Android 6.0 and later): the app adds `android:autoVerify="true"` to an intent filter for `https://shop.example.com`. At install, Android fetches `https://shop.example.com/.well-known/assetlinks.json` and checks that it names the app's package and its signing certificate's **SHA-256 fingerprint** (the value `keytool` printed in lesson 2). Since Android 12, a web link opens in the user's default browser unless the app is approved for that specific domain.
- **iOS Universal Links**: the app's `com.apple.developer.associated-domains` entitlement lists `applinks:shop.example.com`; iOS downloads `https://shop.example.com/.well-known/apple-app-site-association` (the AASA file) and checks that its `appIDs` include the app's Team ID plus bundle ID. The file "must" be served over HTTPS "with no redirects".

Only the domain owner can publish those files, so another app cannot claim the links.

blocks.caption: Both formats follow Android's and Apple's documentation. The fingerprint here is the UnCrackable signing certificate from lesson 2, reused for illustration; a real site lists its own app's fingerprint. ABCDE12345 stands for the developer's Team ID.

scenes.caption: A link is tapped in a message. The operating system decides which app receives it.
Custom scheme shopapp://: any installed app may have declared it. A malicious app that registered the same scheme can be chosen, by the user or by the system.
https link with a verified App Link or Universal Link: the OS checked the domain's file at install. Only the app the domain names can receive it.
Verification answers 'which app'. It does not make the link's contents safe: the code, ids and URLs inside it are still written by whoever made the link.

blocks.md:
**What the app does with the link.** Verified or not, every parameter is attacker-controlled. The MASTG has tests for exactly this: *Missing Input Validation in Custom URL Scheme Handlers* (MASTG-TEST-0394 on Android, 0370 on iOS) and in Universal Link handlers (0395). On Android the MASTG adds that a deep link handler has "no built-in mechanism" to know which app sent the intent; on iOS, Universal Links carry no `sourceApplication` because they come from a web context.

The most dangerous parameter is a URL the app will load or follow, such as `?url=` or `?next=`. Checking it with a partial string comparison is a classic mistake, and Microsoft's advice after the TikTok case (lesson 9) was to "avoid using partial string comparison methods". Compare the two checks below on five inputs.

blocks.caption: Java. Android code usually parses with android.net.Uri; the rule is the same: parse first, then compare whole components.

blocks.code:
$ java LinkCheck
https://shop.example.com/sale              weak=true  fixed=true
https://shop.example.com.evil.test/sale    weak=true  fixed=false
https://evil.test/?next=shop.example.com   weak=true  fixed=false
https://shop.example.com@evil.test/        weak=true  fixed=false
http://shop.example.com/sale               weak=true  fixed=false
blocks.caption: Real output (JDK 25). The weak check passes all five, including a look-alike domain, a query string, a user-info trick (the host is evil.test) and plain HTTP.

blocks.md:
**Deep links and login.** Native apps often receive the OAuth redirect as a deep link. RFC 8252, *OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps* (a Best Current Practice from October 2017), sets the rules:

- Native apps "MUST NOT use embedded user-agents" (a WebView inside the app) for authorization requests, because the host app can read the credentials and cookies typed there. Use the system browser or an in-app browser tab: **Custom Tabs** on Android, `ASWebAuthenticationSession` on iOS, which Apple says "ensures that only the calling app's session receives the authentication callback, even when more than one app registers the same callback URL scheme".
- Prefer a claimed `https` redirect (App Link or Universal Link), whose destination app the OS guarantees. A private-use scheme must be a reversed domain the developer controls, such as `com.example.shop:/oauth2redirect`, and PKCE is still required.

**Defender view.** Prevent: verified links for anything sensitive; validate every parameter against an allowlist; never forward a link's URL into a WebView or an intent. Detect: `adb shell pm get-app-links <package>` shows each domain's verification state on a test device (`verified`, or a failure such as `legacy_failure`); MASTG-TECH-0173 monitors handlers at runtime. Respond: fix the handler server-side where possible (for example, refuse redirects to unknown hosts) so the fix does not wait for every user to update.

blocks.question: An app uses a verified App Link, `https://shop.example.com/open?next=...`, and loads `next` in its WebView after checking `next.startsWith('https://shop.example.com')`. Is it safe?
options: Yes: App Link verification means only trusted links reach the app
No: verification only decides which app receives the link; `https://shop.example.com.evil.test/` and `https://shop.example.com@evil.test/` both pass a prefix check
Yes, because startsWith is stricter than contains
No, because App Links cannot carry query parameters
blocks.explain: Anyone can craft a link to your verified domain with any parameters; verification protects the routing, not the contents. A prefix check fails the same way the contains check did above. Parse the URL and compare scheme and exact host.

blocks.question: Why does RFC 8252 forbid using an in-app WebView for the OAuth login page?
options: WebViews cannot display HTTPS pages
WebViews do not support JavaScript
The app hosting the WebView can read what the user types and the cookies, so a malicious or compromised app could capture the user's credentials for the identity provider
Identity providers block WebView user agents by law
blocks.explain: In an embedded user-agent the host app controls the page and can inspect it, which defeats the point of OAuth (the app should never see the password). The system browser or an in-app browser tab keeps the identity provider's page out of the app's reach.

lessons.title: WebViews: a browser inside the app, with a bridge to native code

blocks.md:
A **WebView** is a browser engine embedded in an app's own screen: Android's `WebView` and iOS's `WKWebView` (from WebKit, the engine behind Safari). Apps use them to show help pages, checkout flows or whole features written as web pages. The appeal is one web codebase for both platforms. The risk is that a web page now runs *inside the app*, and many apps give it a way to call native code.

Tiny example. A shop app shows promotions in a WebView and exposes a bridge object, `account`, so the page can call `account.getToken()` to make logged-in requests. If the WebView only ever loads `https://shop.example.com`, that is the app's own code. If it can be made to load *any* page, every page on the internet can call `getToken()`.

**JavaScript bridges.** On Android, `addJavascriptInterface(obj, "name")` makes a Java object callable from JavaScript as `window.name`. Android's security guidance is blunt about it: the object is injected "into every frame of the WebView, including iframes", and "there is no mechanism for the application to verify the origin of the calling frame". Apps targeting API level 16 or earlier are "particularly at risk", because the page can use the object to control the host app, and before API 21 JavaScript could use reflection on the injected object; today only methods annotated `@JavascriptInterface` are exposed, but those are callable by *any* page loaded.

On iOS, a page calls `window.webkit.messageHandlers.<name>.postMessage(...)`, and the app's `WKScriptMessageHandler` receives a message whose `frameInfo` tells it which frame sent it, with that frame's `securityOrigin` (protocol, host and port). The app can and must check it.

MASWE names the two failures: *Sensitive Native Functionality Exposed in WebViews* (MASWE-0033) and *WebViews Loading Untrusted Content* (MASWE-0035).

**Local files.** A WebView that can read `file://` URLs may let a page read the app's own private files. Android's settings: `setAllowFileAccess()` defaults to **true** for apps targeting API level 29 and lower and **false** from API level 30; the two "from file URLs" settings default to false since API level 16 and were deprecated in API 30; for all three, Android recommends `WebViewAssetLoader`, which serves bundled files under `https://appassets.androidplatform.net/` like a normal site. JavaScript itself is off by default in an Android WebView; turn it on only where needed (MASWE-0034 covers access to local resources).

**Case: TikTok for Android, 2022 (CVE-2022-28799).** Dimitrios Valsamaras of Microsoft's research team reported a chain in TikTok's Android app (both flavours, over 1.5 billion combined installations from Google Play) to TikTok in February 2022. A user tapping one crafted link could have their account hijacked:

1. TikTok exported an https deep link, `https://m.tiktok.com/redirect`, that forwarded a query parameter to other deep links, including internal, non-exported ones.
2. One internal scheme, `<internal>://webview?url=<website>`, loaded a URL into a WebView. A filter rejected untrusted hosts by asking a server; adding two extra parameters to the link bypassed it.
3. That WebView attached a JavaScript bridge exposing "more than 70" methods. Some read or changed private profile data; others made **authenticated HTTP requests** to any URL and returned the reply, headers included.

Microsoft's proof of concept sent the user's video-upload authentication tokens to an attacker's server and changed their profile biography to "!! SECURITY BREACH !!". TikTok shipped a fix less than a month after disclosure (the US National Vulnerability Database, NVD, lists versions before 23.7.3 as affected), and Microsoft found no exploitation in the wild.

blocks.title: TikTok CVE-2022-28799: one tap to an authenticated bridge (simplified)

scenes.caption: The victim taps a crafted https://m.tiktok.com link. TikTok's exported deep link handler receives it, as designed.
The exported redirect handler passes a query parameter on as an internal deep link, reaching a non-exported WebView screen.
A server-side filter should reject untrusted hosts. Two extra parameters in the link bypassed it, so the attacker's page loads.
The WebView has the JavaScript bridge attached. The attacker's script calls a method that makes an authenticated HTTP request with the user's session.
The reply, headers included, is returned to the attacker's script, which forwards tokens to its own server and can change the profile.
Any single fix breaks the chain: no forwarding to internal links, a host check that cannot be bypassed, or a bridge that only answers TikTok's own origin.

blocks.caption: Kotlin. Two independent mistakes: untrusted content in the WebView, and a privileged bridge that cannot tell who is calling.

Kotlin with AndroidX WebKit. addWebMessageListener injects the object only into frames whose origin matches the rules and tells the app the sender's origin, which addJavascriptInterface cannot. Not compiled here.

blocks.md:
**The iOS equivalent.** In a `WKScriptMessageHandler`, check `message.frameInfo.securityOrigin` (and `frameInfo.isMainFrame`) against your own origin before acting, and never build JavaScript strings for `evaluateJavaScript` from untrusted data. The MASTG's iOS tests cover attacker-controlled URLs in WebViews (MASTG-TEST-0332), relaxed file access (0335) and native bridges (0376).

Microsoft's own list after the TikTok case: use an allowlist of trusted domains and open everything else in the default browser; keep the list current and watch for **expiring domains** (an attacker who registers a lapsed allowlisted domain inherits its trust); avoid partial string comparisons; keep staging and internal domains off the list.

**Defender view.** Prevent: no bridge at all where possible; otherwise origin-checked message listeners, an allowlist enforced *before* loading, JavaScript and file access off unless needed, and no login pages in WebViews (lesson 8). Detect: static search for `addJavascriptInterface`, `setJavaScriptEnabled(true)`, `setAllowFileAccess(true)` and `loadUrl` fed from intent data (semgrep rules exist for these); dynamic tests that open your own deep links with external URLs and watch what loads. Respond: a server-side kill switch for the remote content a WebView loads lets you contain a bridge bug before users update.
A WebView bridge turns 'which page is loaded' into 'who can call our native code'. Control both: what may load, and which origin each bridge call came from.

blocks.question: An app's WebView exposes `addJavascriptInterface(Bridge(), 'native')` and loads only `https://help.example.com`. The help site embeds a third-party chat widget in an iframe. What can the widget's script do?
options: Call the bridge's @JavascriptInterface methods, because the object is injected into every frame, including iframes
Nothing: iframes cannot see objects added by the app
Only read the page's text
Call the bridge only if the user taps inside the iframe
blocks.explain: Android's guidance says addJavascriptInterface injects the object into every frame, including iframes, with no way to check the calling frame's origin. Third-party content on your own page therefore reaches your native code. addWebMessageListener with origin rules, or no bridge, fixes it.

blocks.question: In the TikTok chain, which single change would *not* by itself have broken the attack?
options: Stopping the redirect handler from forwarding to internal deep links
Making the host filter impossible to bypass
Restricting the bridge to TikTok's own origin
Making the App Link use a custom scheme instead of https
blocks.explain: Swapping the https link for a custom scheme would not help: any app or page can still trigger a custom-scheme link, and it adds hijacking risk. Each of the other three removes a link in the chain: reaching the WebView, loading the attacker's page, or the page reaching privileged methods.

lessons.title: Local authentication: a fingerprint must unlock a key, not a boolean

blocks.md:
**Local authentication** is the app asking the phone, not the server, to confirm the user is present: a fingerprint, a face scan or the device passcode. Banking apps use it before showing the balance; password managers before revealing a password.

Tiny example. Two apps both show a Face ID prompt before opening a vault. App A receives "success" and sets `unlocked = true`. App B's vault token is encrypted under a key that secure hardware (the Secure Enclave on iPhones) uses only after a real match, so the token is decrypted only then. On a lab device with Frida (lesson 5), a tester can make App A's callback report success without any face; the same trick gets nothing from App B, because no key was released. The MASTG calls A **event-bound** and B **crypto-bound** authentication.

**Why the event-bound kind fails.** The MASTG's iOS test (MASTG-TEST-0266) explains that the LocalAuthentication API "returning only a success or failure result" does not "securely store secrets or enforce any security", making it "susceptible to logic manipulation (e.g., bypassing an `if authenticated` check)". The Keychain, configured to require user presence, makes authentication "part of a secure data retrieval path (out-of-process)". The Android test (MASTG-TEST-0327) says the same of `BiometricPrompt.authenticate()` called without a `CryptoObject`. MASVS puts this under MASVS-AUTH-2; MASWE calls it *Local Authentication Can Be Bypassed* (MASWE-0020).

The platform pieces that make crypto-binding work: on Android, the **Keystore** holds key material that is non-exportable and, where the hardware supports it, bound to a TEE (trusted execution environment) or secure element; a key can be marked as usable only after user authentication. On iOS, the biometric match happens in the **Secure Enclave**, "a hardware-based security processor isolated from the rest of the system", which keeps the authentication data "out of reach even of the operating system".

scenes.caption: Event-bound: the app shows the prompt; the system checks the face or finger and calls the app back with 'success'.
The app's decision is a value in its own memory. On a device the attacker controls, a hook can fire the same callback with no match at all.
Crypto-bound: the token is stored encrypted under a key that the Keystore or Keychain will only use after a fresh biometric match.
The match happens in secure hardware, which then performs the decryption. Only now does the app hold the token.
A faked callback now gains nothing: the key was never used, so the token stays encrypted. The hook would have to defeat the secure hardware itself.

blocks.caption: Kotlin. A hooked or replayed onAuthenticationSucceeded opens the vault, and the token was readable all along.

Kotlin, following Android's biometric guide. The prompt must allow BIOMETRIC_STRONG (Class 3). With a timeout of 0, encrypting the token the first time also needs a prompt (an ENCRYPT_MODE cipher in a CryptoObject). Not compiled here.
Swift, adapted from Apple's article 'Accessing keychain items with Face ID or Touch ID' (which uses .userPresence; .biometryCurrentSet is the stricter flag, see below). Not compiled here.

blocks.md:
**The settings that matter**, each with a MASTG test:

- **Strength.** Android sorts biometrics into Class 3 (`BIOMETRIC_STRONG`) and Class 2 (`BIOMETRIC_WEAK`) by how often they accept spoofs and impostors; crypto-binding needs Class 3.
- **Fallback.** Allowing the device passcode (`DEVICE_CREDENTIAL` on Android, `.deviceOwnerAuthentication` or `.userPresence` on iOS) is convenient, but anyone who has watched the owner type the passcode then passes. For sensitive transactions MASWE-0021 flags it as *Fallback to Non-biometric Credentials Allowed*.
- **Enrollment changes.** If someone adds their own fingerprint to the phone, should they open the vault? With `setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true)` (Android's default for biometric-only keys) or `.biometryCurrentSet` on iOS, the key or item is invalidated when biometrics change; `.userPresence` keeps working. MASWE-0022 covers keys that are not invalidated.
- **Validity window.** A timeout of 0 means authentication per use; a long window lets one unlock cover many operations (MASTG-TEST-0330 checks extended durations).

**Local is not remote.** A biometric prompt proves something to the phone, not to your server. For a server-side action such as a payment, use a key that *signs*: the Keystore or Secure Enclave key signs a server-issued challenge after a biometric match (a `Signature` CryptoObject on Android), and the server verifies the signature with the public key it registered. This is step-up authentication for sensitive actions (MASVS-AUTH-3). Long-lived signing keys are a public-key choice, so plan for migration: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030 and disallows them after 2035.

**Defender view.** Prevent: crypto-bound unlock, Class 3 biometrics, invalidation on enrollment for high-value data. Detect: semgrep rules for `authenticate(` without a CryptoObject and `evaluatePolicy` guarding readable data (MASTG-DEMO-0090 and MASTG-TEST-0266). Respond: move secrets behind Keystore or Keychain access control and rotate any tokens that were stored readable.

Misconception: "we use Face ID, so the data is protected by Face ID." Only if the data is encrypted under a key that requires it. If the token sits in UserDefaults or SharedPreferences, the prompt protects nothing from someone with the device's files (lesson 4) or a hook (lesson 5).

blocks.question: A tester hooks `onAuthenticationSucceeded` and calls it without touching the sensor. The app shows the vault screen, but the account balance stays blank and an error says 'decryption failed'. What does this show?
options: The app is event-bound and vulnerable
Frida is not working
The UI is event-bound, but the data is crypto-bound: the key was never used, so the secret stayed encrypted; worth noting the misleading screen, not a bypass
The biometric sensor is broken
blocks.explain: The vault screen opened on a faked event, but the protected data comes from a cipher that only works after a real match, so the hook gained nothing. That is the crypto-bound design working. The tester may note that the UI should not open before decryption succeeds.

blocks.question: A password manager wants the vault to stop opening if a new fingerprint is added to the phone. Which iOS access control flag fits?
options: .userPresence
.biometryCurrentSet
.devicePasscode
kSecAttrAccessibleAlways
blocks.explain: Apple's documentation: with .biometryCurrentSet the item is invalidated if fingers are added or removed, or Face ID is re-enrolled. .userPresence stays usable after enrollment changes and also accepts the passcode. The last option is not an access control flag for biometrics at all.

lessons.title: The app is not the boundary: backend APIs seen through the app

blocks.md:
Every lesson so far has ended in the same place: the client cannot be trusted with decisions. This lesson tests that idea directly. Once the proxy (lesson 4) shows the app's requests, the tester stops using the app and talks to the API as the app would, asking one question per request: *what does the server enforce, and what did it leave to the app?*

Tiny example. A dating app has a privacy switch, "hide my distance". With it on, the app shows no distance on your profile. The proxy shows that the API response for your profile still contains `"distance": 0.74`; the app simply does not display it. The privacy setting existed only in the user interface.

**A checklist for API tests through the app** (the prerequisite API course taught the underlying bugs: BOLA, excessive data exposure, rate limits):

- **Hidden fields.** Compare each response with what the screen shows. Fields the UI hides are still delivered (excessive data exposure, OWASP API3).
- **Client-side checks.** Anything the app validates (balances, limits, roles, premium flags) must be re-checked by the server. Replay the request with the check removed.
- **Object ids.** Replay requests with a second test account's ids (BOLA, API1). Use two accounts you own.
- **Inputs the app never sends.** Change values the UI cannot produce: negative quantities, other users' locations, a GPS position on another continent.
- **Rate.** Repeat a request quickly. Location queries, one-time password (OTP) checks and coupon redemptions all need server-side limits.

MASVS itself says that for authentication and authorization "the enforcement of these mechanisms must be on the remote endpoint", and points to OWASP's ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard) for the server.
**Case: Grindr location exposure, 2014 to 2019.** Grindr is a location-based dating app for gay and bisexual men, which shows nearby users with their distance.

- **2014.** Synack, a security company, reported two flaws to Grindr in March; its researcher Colby Moore showed that users could be located precisely. Synack wrote ([CSO](https://www.csoonline.com/article/2604777/grindr-vulnerability-places-men-in-harms-way.html)) that the option to disable distance "was only respected in the app's user interface"; the location still reached Grindr's server and could be retrieved by anyone. Reports followed that authorities in Egypt had used the app to locate gay men. In September 2014 Grindr hid distances by default in several countries with anti-gay laws; Synack showed that spoofing the requester's location to Cairo still returned precise distances; a later fix set distance off for those countries in the API, but users elsewhere could still be tracked in real time.
